segments.say: Two products, in two directories, built two different ways. Control Tower, by an interactive agent team with a person in the room. Signal Desk, by a program we wrote, with nobody watching. Same model, same week, same person writing the brief - which is as close to a controlled comparison as anybody is going to get you. The counts are on screen and flatter neither side yet. Control Tower: three commits, forty-eight JavaScript files, four thousand three hundred and ninety-one lines. Signal Desk: four commits, twenty-six files, two thousand three hundred and seventy-six lines. Roughly twice the code on one side, and neither number tells you a thing about whether it works. Lines of code survives as a metric because it is easy to count, not because it means anything. And the framing matters, so let us be exact about what is being compared. Not two models - the same one. Not two briefs - two briefs written the same way by the same person in the same week. And that fourth commit on Signal Desk is the one that just landed - the per-task commit change and the dependency exception, written down. So what we compare includes the corrections we just made. Worth saying out loud, because a comparison that quietly leaves out the fixes is a comparison of two things that no longer exist.

And the numbers, counted the same way on both sides. That is a deliberate small thing: two things measured differently is worse than no numbers at all, and it is the easiest way to accidentally lie in a table. Same command, same exclusions, run over both directories in one loop - the only reason the two rows can sit next to each other at all. Then the instruction, which is written to make a winner difficult. Read both repositories - the plans, the run logs, the review, the test output, the history. Compare them on four things: what each delivered against its own plan, where each went wrong, what each cost in wall-clock time, and which you would reach for, for what kind of work. Ground every claim in a file you read. Where the evidence is missing, say it is missing. And do not decide which is better in general - decide what each is for. And it has to land in a file. Write VERDICT dot md in Signal Desk - not print me a summary, write a document that sits next to the code and can be read again next month. An answer that only exists in a terminal scrollback is one you will retype the question for. And one clause is doing quiet work in the background: where the evidence is missing, say it is missing. Every comparison you have read has a section where the author had nothing and wrote something anyway, because a gap looks like laziness and a paragraph looks like work. Naming the gap is the harder thing to do and the more useful thing to read. And I want to flag one thing about that instruction before the answer comes back, because it is the part I would get wrong if I were doing this quickly. Ground every claim in a file you read is not a politeness. It is the difference between a comparison and a vibe.

That last clause is there because which is better has no answer, and every comparison you have ever watched pretends it does. The team could ask, argue, change its mind and route around a surprise. The program could do none of that, and does not need anybody to be awake. Those are not two grades of the same thing, and a verdict that ranks them has stopped paying attention. Watch what it is actually doing while it thinks. It cats the package file, it reads a stray text file called risky dot txt, it runs git show on the commit that just landed, and then it crosses into the other repository and does the same there. Two and a half minutes in, six files read and eight shell commands run, and not a sentence of the comparison written yet. So this is the last time this week we do the thing the whole week has been about: ask a question that makes a flattering answer difficult, and then read what comes back. And then it does something I did not ask for and should have. It starts Control Tower's server on port eight thousand and eighty and curls it, because reading a repository tells you what somebody wrote and not whether it runs. It also runs both test suites rather than trusting either repository's claim about them. That is the difference between a comparison and a summary of two read-me files, and it is why this is taking minutes instead of seconds. If you have ever been handed a technical comparison that turned out to be a rewrite of both project pages, this is the step that was skipped. There is also a reason to do this at the end of the week rather than the start. Neither of these products existed on Monday. The comparison is not between two tools somebody sells - it is between two things you now know how to build, and the question is not which one wins but which one you reach for on a Tuesday morning with a particular job in front of you.

Six minutes, and it is reading rather than writing for most of them. Two repositories, four documents each, a run log, a review, a test suite and two commit histories. Right now it is grepping the orchestrator source for its phase functions - three minutes and twelve seconds in, eleven thousand tokens pulled. Forty-five seconds later it is inside the other repository reading a git status, a server log, an environment example and a Dockerfile. Not one of those is a document either of us wrote for this comparison. And the reason to give it that long, rather than a summary of each, is the whole argument of this course in one decision: a comparison written from summaries is a comparison of two summaries. And while it reads, the thing worth thinking about is what actually differs between the two builds. It is not capability. It is who notices. In the interactive build a person is in the room, so a surprise gets caught in the second it happens and the plan bends around it - and that costs you a person, present, for the whole run. In the unattended build nobody is there, so a surprise does not get caught at the moment it happens. It gets caught at the end, by whatever you built to check, or it does not get caught at all. So the two failure modes are shaped differently, and that is the part to carry. Supervised work fails visibly and early, in small pieces, while somebody is paying attention. Unattended work fails invisibly and completes anyway, and what comes back is a finished-looking result with something wrong inside it. Neither is worse in the abstract. They are worse in different situations, and knowing which situation you are in is the whole skill. The question is never which machine is better. It is how much it costs you to find out you were wrong. And this is the part of a long agent run I want you to be comfortable with by now, because it is where most people interrupt. Nothing is on screen. It is not stuck.

And here is what it found. Two hundred and forty lines in one pass, after four minutes forty-two of reading and nineteen thousand tokens. Read line four before anything else: every claim below cites the file it came from, and where I looked and found nothing, I say so rather than filling the gap with a guess. Line six says it did not run either app's Docker setup, flagged unverified rather than assumed. That is the document telling you where not to trust it, before you ask. On time, it will not give me the headline I wanted. The program's build has a machine-generated record - seventeen minutes and fifty-two seconds of unattended execution for six areas, and fifty-one minutes from the first commit to the last, including planning, review and the fix pass. The team's has no equivalent, because nothing logged it: three commits spanning six hours and fourteen minutes, and that is all the evidence there is. And it says plainly that those two numbers are not comparable - one is machine-measured agent execution and the other is wall clock across a supervised session with a person thinking in it. Then it says what neither repository records at all, which is what either of them cost in money. That is a gap in our own work, found by something reading it. Notice what it does with the missing evidence, too. It does not estimate the cost, it does not extrapolate from token counts, and it does not quietly leave the section out.

And then two findings about Control Tower that nobody in that six-hour session caught. The finished work is still sitting on an unmerged branch. And the Agent SDK dependency went into the wrong field of the package file. Main has only the first commit. Everything else lives on a branch called agent-team, so the finished build was never merged. And the plan file still says most of the app is unbuilt, which stopped being true hours before anybody stopped working. Both are the sort of thing a review catches in thirty seconds - and there was no review, because a person was in the room, and a person in the room feels like one. And I want to be clear that those are our defects, in work I supervised, found by a program reading it in six minutes. It is not one-sided either. On the Signal Desk side it flags a file called risky dot txt that arrived in the final commit with no reference anywhere in the codebase and no mention in the commit message. Nobody knows what it is for. That is what an unattended run leaves behind: not a crash, an unexplained artefact, in a build disciplined enough to write its own review. That is not an argument for unattended pipelines over people. It is an argument that whatever you build with, the last step is somebody or something reading the repository against what you said you wanted.

Which gives it a conclusion I did not expect and would not have written. A person being present did not substitute for a review. It substituted for some of one, and missed exactly the things the program's automated review step is built to catch. And the document spares neither side. Section two is headed where each went wrong, and both names appear under it. That is the shape to copy: not a winner and a loser, a list of what each one actually did to you. So the recommendation is not to pick a side. It is to take the one piece of process the unattended pipeline has - a read-only agent that checks the repository against the plan when the work stops - and bolt it onto the interactive way of working as well. What made the unattended build trustworthy was never the agents.
